chunks: "Both decompose a signal into sinusoids, but they apply to different kinds of signals. The Fourier series is for periodic signals.
A periodic signal with period T can be written as a sum of sinusoids at the fundamental frequency, 1 over T , and its integer multiples, the harmonics.
So the spectrum is discrete: lines at specific frequencies, each with a coefficient. A square wave, for instance, has only odd harmonics with amplitudes that fall as one over n.
The Fourier transform is for aperiodic signals, like a single pulse or a decaying transient, which don't repeat.
Because there's no fundamental, the spectrum is continuous: every frequency can have content, and you get a spectral density rather than discrete lines.
They're two sides of the same idea.
If you take a pulse and repeat it every T seconds, you get a series whose coefficients are samples of the pulse's Fourier transform, spaced 1 over T apart.
As the period goes to infinity, the lines get closer and merge into the continuous transform.
And the transform of a periodic signal is itself a train of impulses at the harmonics.
In practice, instruments compute the discrete transform of a finite record, which implicitly treats it as one period of a periodic signal.
That's why if the record isn't an integer number of cycles you get leakage."
